content: 1. Among the participants in the FTC-TDF study arm, 151 out of 1251 patients (12%) reported experiencing a grade 3 or 4 adverse event. In comparison, 164 out of 1248 patients (13%) in the control arm reported similar adverse events. This difference was not statistically significant. 2. Project PrEPare documented six adverse events in total, five of which were deemed possibly or probably related to the study drug. All of these events occurred in the FTC-TDF study arm. 3. The iPrEx study observed that both the FTC-TDF and control groups reported increased condom use during receptive intercourse over the course of the intervention. However, the differences in condom use rates between the two groups were not statistically significant. 4. A linear mixed regression model was employed to analyze the relationship between treatment and outcomes. This model included a random intercept and fixed effects for treatment visit and treatment-by-visit interaction. The p-value derived from a Wald test assessed whether there was a difference between the FTC-TDF and control groups during the study period. 5. The change in the proportion of men reporting unprotected anal sex (UAS) from baseline to months 3-9 was similar between the immediate and delayed intervention groups. Percentages of participants reporting UAS in the past month at baseline and week 24 were 42% and 42% for the PrEP arm, 40% and 10% for the placebo arm, and 31% and 23% for the no-pill arm. There was a non-significant trend of decreasing UAS across all treatment arms from baseline to week 24. 6. In the iPrEx study, the number of receptive sexual intercourse partners declined from baseline to follow-up in both study arms. However, there was no significant difference in the number of partners reported between the study groups at any time point. 7. The Kenya intermittent PrEP study reported slight changes in the number of sexual partners over time but did not assess statistical significance. 8. The CDC safety study and Project PrEPare both found a decrease in unprotected sex over time, with no significant differences across study arms. Similarly, the CDC safety study observed a reduction in the number of sexual partners over time, with no significant differences between groups. 9. Awareness of PrEP among men who have sex with men (MSM) remains limited globally, although studies suggest an increase in awareness since the release of the iPrEx results. Willingness to use PrEP varies widely across studies, with most reporting willingness rates between 40-70%. Barriers to PrEP use include concerns about effectiveness, side effects, cost, accessibility, mistrust of healthcare providers, stigma, and risk compensation. 10. Healthcare providers generally express awareness and support for PrEP, but fewer have prescribed it. Concerns among providers include drug resistance, risk compensation, poor adherence, lack of local guidelines, and the fit of PrEP within current care models that do not include frequent clinic visits. 11. Cost-effectiveness studies of PrEP among MSM, primarily conducted in the US, Australia, and Peru, show varying results. In the US and Australia, estimates range from PrEP being cost-saving to costing over $300,000 per QALY saved. In Peru, PrEP could be a cost-effective addition to MSM prevention programs at $1,702-$2,755 per DALY saved, below the WHO-recommended threshold for cost-effective interventions. 12. Oral PrEP for MSM has been shown to be feasible in various trial settings and acceptability studies, including among young MSM. However, issues such as criminalization, stigma, discrimination, and violence should be considered during implementation, especially in regions where MSM behavior is illegal. 13. Since 2011, the number of studies describing values and preferences for PrEP use among MSM has increased dramatically. Most participants in these studies were HIV-negative or of unknown serostatus. Awareness of PrEP has increased since the iPrEx study results but remains limited. Willingness to use PrEP has generally been high, though it varies across studies. 14. Barriers to PrEP use commonly include concerns about effectiveness, side effects, and cost. Some studies report that participants anticipate changing their sexual behavior, such as reducing condom use, as a result of using PrEP. 15. Healthcare provider perspectives on PrEP for MSM reveal that most providers are aware of and support PrEP, but few have prescribed it. Barriers to prescribing include concerns about antiretroviral resistance, risk compensation, poor adherence, and lack of local guidelines.
